articles.body:
The Republican National Committee announced Monday that President Trump will campaign in Rock Hill, S.C., on Thursday, marking his second trip to the Palmetto State within the span of a week.

Trump campaigned last week in Clemson, in an effort to boost Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) in her race against Democrat Annie Andrews.

The campaign stop will take place in the Charlotte, N.C., media market, given Rock Hill’s location on the North Carolina border, meaning the visit will likely also be used to boost Republican Michael Whatley in his Senate race against former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper (D).

Trump campaigned Tuesday for Whatley in Greenville, N.C.

Both Senate races have become increasingly competitive in the last few weeks before Election Day. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates North Carolina’s Senate race as “likely Democrat” and moved South Carolina’s Senate race from “likely Republican” to lean Republican” last week.

Trump’s trip to Rock Hill is the latest in a series of trips he is taking in the final week before Election Day. Trump is slated to visit Mississippi on Monday, Texas on Tuesday, Ohio on Wednesday and Florida on Friday. The president will also campaign in Iowa on Sunday.

articles.title: Billy Crystal: Trump’s Kennedy Center moves ‘so selfish and so petty’
articles.summary: Billy Crystal — the recipient of two of the Kennedy Center’s most prestigious awards — says what’s happening at the Washington performing arts institution amid President Trump’s legal battle “really hurts.” “I’m one of the few who has been awarded the Mark Twain Prize and the Kennedy Honor with an elite group of people that…
articles.body:
Billy Crystal — the recipient of two of the Kennedy Center’s most prestigious awards — says what’s happening at the Washington performing arts institution amid President Trump’s legal battle “really hurts.”

“I’m one of the few who has been awarded the Mark Twain Prize and the Kennedy Honor with an elite group of people that I don’t feel I belong with, but it’s astounding,” Crystal said in an interview on MS NOW’s “Connect with Jacob Soboroff” on Saturday. “And so my affection for it and my respect for it is enormous.”

Crystal received the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor in 2007 and was among the Kennedy Center honorees in 2023.

“I remember sitting next to Queen Latifah — next to the president and the first lady — and looking at the names of the prior winners that we were now a part of, and it was astounding,” the “When Harry Met Sally” star recalled, before criticizing Trump without mentioning him by name.

“So to see it being defiled, and being just thrown around like a commodity, as, ‘It’s mine, it’s mine,’ I just don’t get that. And it really hurts to see that happen,” Crystal, 78, said.

Asked by Soboroff for his reaction when Trump “wanted to put his name on there,” Crystal replied, shaking his head, “I just went, ‘No.'”

“It’s just so selfish and just so petty,” said Crystal, who’s performing on Broadway in his one-man show, “860.”

The comedic actor’s comments come after the president declined in recent weeks to commit to not demolishing the Kennedy Center as the legal fight over its name and renovation plays out.

Last year, Trump named himself the chair of the Kennedy Center’s board, firing several members and installing a handpicked slate of administration officials and allies.

That November, the board voted to add the president’s name to the facade of the building. The move was later reversed by a federal judge. Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio board member, has since led a legal challenge over the Kennedy Center changes.

The Kennedy Center is closed temporarily for renovations, as officials say the building is in serious disrepair and unsafe for visitors.

This year’s 49th annual Kennedy Center Honors, which typically take place in December, will be held at Washington’s Capital One Arena.

articles.title: Judge orders DOJ to reinstate former federal prosecutor Maurene Comey, daughter of ex-FBI director
articles.summary: A federal judge ruled Monday that former Assistant United States Attorney Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, was “unlawfully terminated” and ordered that she be reinstated.
articles.body: A federal judge ruled Monday that former Assistant United States Attorney Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, was “unlawfully terminated” and ordered that she be reinstated. The Justice Department’s abrupt firing of Comey in July 2025 violated the Constitution’s separation of powers and her Fifth Amendment due process and statutory rights, U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman found. The Trump administration’s assertion that it can fire career prosecutors at will would “unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system,” the judge wrote. He granted Comey back pay effective from the date of her termination through Dec. 20, 2025, when she began a new job. A spokesperson for the Justice Department said DOJ “disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course.” In a joint statement, Comey’s attorneys Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan said that “this decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law.” They added that the “hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law.” Comey had worked on a number of high-profile cases in the Southern District of New York, including the prosecutions of disgraced music mogul Sean “Diddy” Combs, former Sen. Bob Menendez, D-N.J., and the late financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his co-conspirator, Ghislaine Maxwell. Comey filed suit in September 2025, alleging the Trump administration provided “no legitimate explanation” for firing her after almost 10 years of service, and that it had only done so because of President Donald Trump’s “well-known and longstanding vendetta against James Comey, whom he fired as FBI Director in 2017.” Maurene Comey said the only thing she was told about her firing from her boss was that it “came from Washington.” The Justice Department later said in a court filing that she was removed at the direction of then-Attorney General Pam Bondi. The judge found Bondi did not follow the law when she fired Comey, depriving Comey of her rights to due process. “Congress granted the Attorney General power to remove Comey,” the judge wrote, but “Congress imposed limits on that power — limits that, even Defendants concede, were violated in Comey’s case.” Among DOJ’s arguments were that Bondi had the authority to fire Comey “at will” and for no reason at all, and that Congress does not have the authority to put limits on that authority. Furman roundly rejected those arguments. DOJ has staked out a “sweeping and unprecedented theory of executive authority,” he wrote, and its position “flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent.” The Trump administration has routinely fired career federal prosecutors along with FBI employees, particularly focusing on individuals involved in prior investigations of Trump or with the massive investigation into the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. Furman seemed to take note of those firings while declaring Comey’s firing unlawful. “Defendants invented a new and expansive theory of executive power. And they have also utilized that theory to remove other Executive Branch employees who have long held protections from removal,” he wrote, adding the declaration should “serve a useful purpose in clarifying or settling the legal issues involved.” The administration is also continuing to push forward with a federal criminal case brought against Comey’s father over a photo of seashells that it contends amounted to a threat against Trump. The seashells case has been delayed until at least early 2027 as a judge weighs whether to dismiss it. James Comey’s team has argued the case is a product of Trump’s retribution campaign rather than a good faith application of federal law and that “dictionaries, context, precedent, and common sense” show the seashells photo was not a true threat.

articles.title: Judge rules James Comey’s daughter unlawfully fired as federal prosecutor
articles.summary: A federal judge ruled Monday that the Department of Justice (DOJ) unlawfully fired and must provide back pay to Maurene Comey, former FBI Director James Comey’s daughter who was terminated as a prosecutor last year. U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman rejected the Trump administration’s arguments that it had constitutional authority to fire her. “Defendants’ argument is contrary…
articles.body:
A federal judge ruled Monday that the Department of Justice (DOJ) unlawfully fired and must provide back pay to Maurene Comey, former FBI Director James Comey’s daughter who was terminated as a prosecutor last year.

U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman rejected the Trump administration’s arguments that it had constitutional authority to fire her .

“Defendants’ argument is contrary to an unbroken line of Supreme Court decisions dating back almost two centuries, and the Supreme Court itself has not formally overruled any of those decisions. That is sufficient, in itself, to reject the argument,” Furman wrote in his 55-page opinion .

Maurene Comey has since taken another job and won’t be returning to the DOJ. But the judge’s ruling retroactively reinstates her, provides her with back pay and restores pension benefits for the four-month period before she took that new role. It also orders an update to her personnel file to reflect that she resigned instead of saying she was fired.

“The Department disagrees with this decision, which obstructs President Trump’s constitutional authority to fire individuals who wield executive power on his behalf. We intend to appeal the decision in due course,” the Justice Department wrote on X .

Comey sued last year after DOJ officials informed her that July she was being removed from her role as a criminal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York. She says it was because of her perceived political affiliation and her connection to her father, whom Trump fired as FBI director in 2017, which sparked the appointment of special counsel Robert Mueller to take over the Russia investigation.

James Comey has become a vocal foe of the president in the years since, and the DOJ is prosecuting him for posting last year an image of seashells spelling “86 47,” arguing it was a violent threat against the president.

Furman’s ruling doesn’t address those First Amendment arguments. Instead, the appointee of former President Obama ruled that Maurene Comey’s firing violated restrictions Congress has enacted for terminating assistant U.S. attorneys.

The DOJ has argued such limits are unconstitutional — pointing to the Supreme Court’s recent decision invalidating Congress’s firing protections for independent agency leaders — but the judge said that’s limited to principal officers and does not impact the protections for people like Comey.

“Defendants’ contention that recent Supreme Court decisions have fatally undermined that precedent is not one that this Court, as a lower court, may accept. It is also without merit,” Furman wrote. “Indeed, to accept Defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.”

In a statement, Comey’s lawyers said the decision reaffirms “our bedrock system of checks and balances.” “This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law,” they said.

articles.title: Backlash after Trump invokes 9/11 in attack on El-Sayed
articles.summary: The Democrat himself has hit back, as has Senator Bernie Sanders and a key Trump supporter from 2024.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump is facing a backlash after invoking 9/11 as part of a verbal assault on Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Michigan.

Speaking at a rally in the state on Sunday, Trump accused El-Sayed of being "a jihadist". He introduced as a guest speaker the father of a passenger who fought back against the 9/11 hijackers.

Trump also suggested that El-Sayed would "have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate".

Critics condemned Trump's attack as Islamophobic. El-Sayed himself responded to Trump's decision to refer to him by his middle name, Mohamed, saying during a rally of his own: "I'll be Senator Mohamed to you, bro."

He also said: "They think that by pointing at my name and my faith, that somehow you're going to ignore the fact that you can't afford your gas or your groceries, can't see a doctor."

Appearing alongside him, Senator Bernie Sanders said: "The reason they are using Islamophobia against Abdul is because they have nothing to say about the real issues."

El-Sayed is taking on Republican candidate Mike Rogers on 3 November. The race is expected to be one of the closest in the midterm elections, and is proving to be particularly bitter.

The seat is considered to be one of just a handful that could decide the balance of power in Congress. It is currently held by the Democrats.

El-Sayed, a former public health official who was born in the US to Egyptian parents, will be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate if he wins the seat.

He has previously dismissed the various attacks made against him by both Trump and Rogers and denied any connection to extremist groups.

Michigan Senate debate spotlights increase in anti-Muslim rhetoric as midterms race heats up

Rapper Nicki Minaj joins Trump onstage at Michigan rally

During his remarks on Sunday, Trump said: "If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas."

Trump made a variety of allegations against El-Sayed and his family members, including that he was a member of the Muslim Brotherhood.

He introduced as a guest speaker the father of Todd Beamer, a man from Michigan who was part of a group of passengers who fought back against the hijackers of United Airlines Flight 93, before the plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania.

"Michigan needs to stand up and fight, just like Todd did, to stop a jihadist from walking into the Capitol," Trump said.

Claims centre on proscribed Muslim Brotherhood

El-Sayed's opponents have sought to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist organisation that was founded in Egypt. Trump designated certain chapters of it as Foreign Terrorist Organisations earlier this year.

Some of the scrutiny of the affiliations of El-Sayed and his family members relates to their writings from more than a decade ago.

A social media post in 2012 by El-Sayed's half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, appeared to refer to the movement, saying "my family has long been MB". El-Sayed's team have previously distanced him from other comments by Abdelhadi.

Critics have also pointed to an opinion piece El-Sayed wrote in Huffington Post in 2011 about pro-democracy protesters in Egypt. In it, he acknowledged concerns that "supporting democracy in Egypt might allow the country to fall to the hands of the Muslim Brotherhood".

A year later he also allegedly signed an open letter by Egyptian Americans. In it, the group urged Mohamed Morsi, Egypt's first democratically elected president and a leader of the Muslim Brotherhood, to "purge the media and police" following the toppling of the authoritarian regime in the Arab Spring. This letter has not been discussed by El-Sayed.

El-Sayed has previously denied any connection to the Muslim Brotherhood and has stressed his loyalty to the United States. Asked recently at a town hall event whether he would disavow the organisation, he responded: "Absolutely."

Also in 2012, El-Sayed's current opponent Rogers, who was then a US representative and chairing the House Intelligence Committee, appeared to call for cautious engagement with the Muslim Brotherhood, telling Reuters : "Do I think there are moderate Muslim Brotherhood individuals we are going to have to reach out to and talk to? Yes but we are going to have to watch it carefully."

HA Hellyer, senior associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) and an expert on Egypt, says the row has more to do with Islamophobia on the political right in the US than with the Trump administration's actual position on the Muslim Brotherhood.

"If the accusation is to be taken sincerely, then [Trump] should surely have a problem with engaging with any government that has engaged positively with the Brotherhood or with groups that are even more to the right of the Brotherhood," Hellyer told the BBC. "He clearly has not done that."

Among the others who condemned Trump's attacks were one of his key supporters ahead of the 2024 presidential election.

"The president's statements are out of line," Bishara Bahbah told the Associated Press. "They are crossing a red line. They are racist."

Bahbah was the founder of Arab Americans for Trump, a group believed to have been important in helping the president connect with a wider range of voters two years ago. The group later changed its name, removing the reference to Trump.

Trump clinched the White House in 2024 after victories in Michigan, which has a prominent population of Arab Americans, and a number of other swing states.

Asked about accusations of Islamophobia, White House spokesman Davis Ingle said: "Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed wants to massively raise taxes, advocates for defunding the police, and wants to destroy the Michigan auto industry by banning gasoline powered vehicles.

"President Trump will continue to call out complete and total extremists like El-Sayed without apology."

Additional reporting by Jake Horton and Tom Bateman

articles.title: California has become unaffordable — but Congress can do something about it
articles.summary: California Reps. Vince Fong and James Gallagher introduced two joint resolutions to overturn the California Air Resources Board’s Vessels At-Berth and Commercial Harbor Craft regulations, which they argue act as hidden climate taxes increasing costs for consumers.
articles.body:
Under Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom’s policies, California continues to be one of the most expensive places to live and do business. We pay some of the nation’s highest prices for gas and electricity. California families pay nearly $2 more per gallon than the national average for gas and more than $8 per gallon for diesel.

Housing is unaffordable. Taxes are out of control. And the goods families depend on keep getting more expensive.

Instead of addressing this affordability crisis, Sacramento is making it worse.

The California Air Resources Board is an unelected state agency that has imposed two mandates most working Californians have probably never heard of. These mandates are raising the cost of everything, from gas to groceries. In essence, they function as a hidden climate tax that gets passed directly to consumers.

They are the “Vessels At-Berth” rule and the “Commercial Harbor Craft” rule. Most don’t know they exist, but every hardworking family feels the impacts at the gas pump or the supermarket.

The Vessels At-Berth regulation requires ships in California ports to shut off their engines and use California Air Resources Board-approved emission-control technology. The problem: the technology is costly and even if ships want to comply, the technology doesn’t exist at the scale needed. The result is fines of around $50,000 per vessel per day , which ultimately gets passed on to consumers in the form of higher prices at checkout.

Similarly, the Commercial Harbor Craft regulation forces operators to install expensive new equipment on vessels like fishing boats. Shipping companies then pass those expenses through the supply chain.

With these two mandates, working families end up paying a tax they never voted for and will never see listed on a receipt.

California Air Resources Board’s own analysis pegs the cost of its At-Berth mandate at $2.3 billion , and its Commercial Harbor Craft rule would pile on more than $2.5 billion , costs that land on maritime operators and, ultimately, consumers.

While Sacramento keeps making life more costly and more unaffordable, we are fighting to cut costs for Californians.

That is why we introduced two joint resolutions . Thanks to the leadership of House Republicans, both resolutions passed the House of Representatives.

Our legislation would overturn these mandates and provide relief to working Californians. They are about commonsense and affordability. The stakes are significant.

These mandates hit the vessels that keep California’s ports and economy operating. We should be helping them save costs and run efficiently, not crushing them with hidden climate taxes.

California’s ports are critical to the Central Valley and Northern California. Removing measures that limit the movement of goods through our ports will support local businesses, keep our supply chains moving, and ultimately bring down costs across the board.

The truth is simple. We all depend on California’s ports . Nearly 40 percent of all containerized cargo entering the nation passes through them. When Sacramento makes shipping more expensive, families in California and across the country pay the price.

Clean air and affordable living should not be competing goals. Californians deserve both.

The House has acted. Now the Senate must pass these resolutions and send them to the president’s desk.

We will keep fighting to stop Sacramento’s hidden climate taxes from taking more hard-earned money from working families.

Vince Fong represents California’s 20th Congressional District and James Gallagher represents California’s 1st Congressional District in the U.S. House of Representatives.

articles.title: Trump administration sued over refugee policy changes
articles.summary: Advocacy groups are suing the Trump administration over three policies they say have left refugees in “legal limbo” by blocking them from obtaining green cards and speeding up the process for terminating their lawful status. The class action lawsuit, filed Monday in Massachusetts, accuses the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration…
articles.body:
Advocacy groups are suing the Trump administration over three policies they say have left refugees in “legal limbo” by blocking them from obtaining green cards and speeding up the process for terminating their lawful status.

The class action lawsuit , filed Monday in Massachusetts, accuses the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) of violating federal immigration law by launching “coordinated attacks” against refugees who have resettled in the U.S. and already been vetted.

“This lawsuit challenges these actions, which, taken together, keep refugees from obtaining lawful permanent residency—a status to which they are statutorily entitled—and place them at risk of termination of their refugee status with no meaningful opportunity to be heard,” the complaint states.

The Trump administration ordered immigration officers in November to re-vet all refugees who were admitted under the Biden administration, placing an indefinite hold on all pending green card applications.

The lawsuit blasted the reinterview process as a “baseless fishing expedition,” noting refugees are among the most thoroughly screened and vetted immigrants who come to the country.

Earlier this month, the DHS also adopted a new rule that shortens the window for a refugee to appeal the proposed termination of their status from 30 to 10 days. The rule cites the need to “restore integrity to the immigration system,” protect national security and prevent fraud as the rationale for speeding up the process.

But the lawsuit argues that the cut doesn’t leave refugees enough time to challenge the revocation of their status, stripping them of constitutional due process rights.

“These actions are the latest in a systematic effort to implement policies that are hostile to refugees, with the end goal of terminating their refugee status and expelling refugees en masse,” lawyers for the plaintiffs wrote.

The Hill has reached out to the USCIS for comment.

The lawsuit was brought on behalf of refugee advocacy organizations and four individual refugees from Afghanistan, Colombia, Ethiopia and Iraq who say their applications for lawful permanent status are still pending.

It asks a federal judge to block the policies from being enforced while the broader legal challenge plays out, including an immediate pause to the new refugee status rule.

“These are people who fled persecution, underwent years of rigorous vetting, and have built lives, families, and communities in the United States,” said Skye Perryman, the president and CEO of Democracy Forward, in a statement. Democracy Forward is one of the groups representing the plaintiffs.

Since President Trump returned to the White House, the administration has sought to drastically reduce the number of refugees admitted to the U.S. by overhauling the federal refugee program.

It has proposed a cap of 17,500 people for the coming year under the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program, which the president argues should be primarily reserved for white South Africans.

articles.title: ‘Cheesecake Factory’: Obama trashes Trump despite numerous failures
articles.summary: Who does Obama think he is?
articles.body:
Ex-President Obama is unloading on current President Trump, in support of Democrats vying to take back the Senate. He had some line about the Cheesecake Factory, which people thought was funny, for some reason. Why exactly? I’m not sure. Maybe you can tell me. Let’s watch.

“Like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” Huh. I don’t get it? What’s the catch?

Saddam Hussein, may I remind you, was a reprehensible dictator of Iraq, who was overthrown by America, under Republican leadership. Obama, then a state senator, objected to this very thing, you may recall. If he didn’t like Hussein’s industrial policy, he certainly failed to speak up about it. But that’s fine, whatever. Now it’s a punch line.

Now he says Trump, who is carrying out much needed and entirely reasonable renovations of the White House, is akin to a dictator for that reason? Well that doesn’t make sense.

Let me remind you that every president has made changes to the White House grounds, and often they are needed. The ballroom is something the president absolutely has the right to build, and it serves a vital function. Who does Obama think he is? This man loves to be the center of attention. He adores the attention he receives from mainstream and liberal media.

And also, excuse me, why is the Cheesecake Factory suddenly an object of ridicule? This is a wonderful American institution. There is something for everyone, and that’s great. Variety is an essential component of the free market system. It’s a good thing. We celebrate it.

Honestly, I’m not surprised that Obama would make fun of it. He is a spokesperson for the far left, for an anti-capitalism economic system, in which choice is undervalued. Let the central committee decide what main course you get, screw the menu. That’s his whole philosophy. I don’t miss it — do you, fellow voters? Do we really want to elect the most radical, far-left pro-socialist majority to ever aspire to hold power in American history? That sounds far more dangerous to me than letting Donald Trump add a new wing to the White House — a space that will be enjoyed by Republican and Democratic administrations for years to come.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Greene says ‘Trump has become a curse to Republican candidates’ ahead of Election Day

Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) criticized President Trump, saying Sunday he had “become a curse to Republican candidates” ahead the November midterm elections when the GOP is projected to lose the House. “He has no idea how bad he is doing in GA. And to threaten our state that he would refuse to help…
articles.body:
Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) criticized President Trump, saying Sunday he had “become a curse to Republican candidates” ahead the November midterm elections when the GOP is projected to lose the House.

“He has no idea how bad he is doing in GA. And to threaten our state that he would refuse to help the good people of Georgia just because he doesn’t like who calls him shows how much he really doesn’t care,” Greene wrote on social media in response to Trump delivering remarks at a campaign rally in the Peach State.

“Trump has become a curse to Republican candidates and it will be worse in ‘28,” she concluded.

The clip Greene responded to showed Trump saying there was “a big difference” when a president “likes the people representing his name.”

“Collins could call me anytime he wants ,” Trump said about Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), who is running for Georgia’s Senate seat. “There’s a big difference between that and Pee Wee Herman calling. Sir, Pee Wee Herman’s like, tell him I’m not in. I’m not in. But he needs money for Georgia. I don’t give a damn what he wants. I’m not in.”

Once a Trump ally, Greene lost the president’s endorsement last November. She resigned from Congress in January during a feud with the president.

The tiff concerned Trump’s handling of files linked to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and a perceived lack of attention from the president on bringing down costs. In April, she stated she believed that Trump was “ not the same man that we supported ” for a decade.

Greene’s comments come as the GOP attempts to navigate a rocky midterm environment amid growing dissatisfaction with Trump’s war in Iran and the cost of living. At the same time, Trump’s approval rating fell to a historic low , according to a New York Times/Siena poll.

articles.title: House Democrats call for special counsel to investigate Trump’s ties to Epstein
articles.summary: Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee are calling for a special counsel to investigate President Trump’s alleged ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, in a report released Monday. Democrats claimed that out of the 11 women who have tied Trump to Epstein’s crimes of sexual abuse and exploitation, five of them have “directly accused…
articles.body:
Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee are calling for a special counsel to investigate President Trump’s alleged ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, in a report released Monday.

Democrats claimed that out of the 11 women who have tied Trump to Epstein’s crimes of sexual abuse and exploitation, five of them have “directly accused Trump of raping or sexually assaulting them in Epstein’s company or direct physical presence.”

It goes further to note that Trump has denied any ties to Epstein’s operations and alleges Attorney General Todd Blanche is covering up “further evidence that directly implicates Trump.”

“Instead of pursuing justice for Epstein’s survivors, former Attorney General Pam Bondi and Attorney General Blanche have been running DOJ like a private legal defense firm for their former client,” the report says. “Determined to protect the President at any cost, DOJ itself now leads the cover-up of Epstein’s sex trafficking operation. Todd Blanche has gone from being Donald Trump’s personal attorney to his personal Attorney General.”

Democrats said in the report that a special counsel is needed to investigate not only Trump’s ties to Epstein, but also all of Epstein’s co-conspirators and to hold the individuals accountable in criminal proceedings.

“Donald Trump says he knew Jeffrey Epstein ‘just like everybody in Palm Beach knew him.’ Not exactly. Evidence involving 11 women tells a completely different and far more damning story about their relationship and the abuse of young women and girls that took place in their network,” House Judiciary Committee ranking member Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) said in a statement.

Bondi testified before the House Judiciary Committee on the Epstein files in February. During that hearing, she argued that “there is no evidence that Donald Trump has committed a crime.”

Democrats also made a point then of noting how many times Trump’s name appears in the files, particularly after FBI Director Kash Patel previously asserted it was fewer than 1,000.

Trump has previously sought to distance himself from Epstein, arguing he was not “friendly” with him, and that he’s never been to Epstein’s private island or been on Epstein’s plane. He even said at one point that he turned down an offer to go to Epstein’s island.

Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, told The Hill that “none of these allegations” in the report are true.

“This ‘report’ is nothing more than a desperate attempt by crazed Democrats to distract Americans from the surging Republican momentum driven by President Trump’s historic achievements. The President kicked Jeffrey Epstein out of his club at Mar-a-Lago because he was a creep, and he has been fully exonerated of anything related to Epstein,” she said.

articles.title: Mike Rogers deflects as Kristen Welker presses him on if he’s ‘MAGA’
articles.summary: Rogers wants Trump’s endorsement without necessarily owning Trump’s agenda, and so from now until Election Day, it seems the strategy is deflect, deflect, deflect.
articles.body:
Kristen Welker asked Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers three times whether he considers himself a MAGA Republican on “Meet The Press” Sunday. And three times, he found a way around the question.

Welker : “Let me just ask you, big picture, do you consider yourself to be a MAGA Republican?”

Rogers : “I get you guys on the national press, but this is a little bit disgusting to me. You know what you don’t cover? The chairman of the Democrat Party just came out and said he cannot, the former chairman, sorry, he cannot vote for ….”

Welker: “Hold on, Congressman, I’m asking you about you.”

So why is a Trump-endorsed candidate suddenly so uncomfortable answering that question?

Ohhhhh, because Rogers declined to endorse Trump in 2016 or 2020, then endorsed him in 2024. Now, with control of the Senate potentially riding on Michigan, that relationship seems a lot more complicated since the president’s favorability rating is so low and Michiganders, like many people across the country, are looking for the country to head in a new direction. The Trump brand was an asset in the primary but it’s seemingly become a liability in the general election.

Look at the messaging. Trump endorsed Rogers, promising a partner on his “America First” agenda, emphasizing the economy as one area they would work closely together, but Rogers’s own campaign is now challenging one of Trump’s signature economic policies — tariffs.

This is such a flip flop. Rogers spent months defending Trump’s tariffs, saying as recently as September that “President Trump is right to put America First – and tariffs are necessary.” But he must have forgotten that Michigan’s economy is deeply connected to Canada, and the trade fight is now a political problem.

The president is finally realizing that his tariffs on Canada were not a great idea, since the administration recently announced that it’s now moving to exempt some Canadian products from tariffs starting on Oct. 30, with The Wall Street Journal reporting that this was a move to help vulnerable Republicans, including Susan Collins in Maine.

Republicans are increasingly keeping Trump out of their general-election advertising after whole-heartedly embracing him in the primaries. A CNBC analysis of AdImpact data shows his mentions falling from 47.1 percent around the primaries to just 4.3 percent now.

The race is extremely tight, Decision Desk HQ polling shows Abdul El-Sayed with a narrow lead over Rogers . Michigan’s in-person early voting began Saturday.

And Trump, himself, is escalating his input in this race, attacking former President Obama just for campaigning with El-Sayed recently. In a Truth Social post at almost 1am Sunday morning, Trump called Obama “a grossly incompetent President!” and labeled El-Sayed “a Muslim Brotherhood Jihadist.”

Obama had the perfect response to these attacks on El-Sayed’s name and religion, reminding folks that Trump often intentionally uses fear to sow division and “may even use your name, or your faith, to somehow suggest that you are dangerous and less than trustworthy and less patriotic and less American.” And then he left us all with a mic drop moment : “We have seen this movie before. I starred in it. I’ve got a long form birth certificate to prove it. This stuff didn’t work on me, not in Michigan. It’s not going to work on Abdul.”

Rogers wants Trump’s endorsement without necessarily owning Trump’s agenda, and so from now until Election Day, it seems the strategy is deflect, deflect, deflect and make Abdul El-Sayed’s name and religion the boogyman instead of owning up to policy decisions that have hurt Michigan voters.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: 6 citizens sue Trump over White House bans on news outlets
articles.summary: Six individual citizens — a civics teacher, a legal journalist, a student journalist, a human rights advocate, a historian and a media watchdog — are suing the president and Trump administration officials over the White House’s bans and restrictions on the press, according to the lawsuit filed Monday. The complaint, which named President Trump alongside…
articles.body:
Six individual citizens — a civics teacher, a legal journalist, a student journalist, a human rights advocate, a historian and a media watchdog — are suing the president and Trump administration officials over the White House’s bans and restrictions on the press, according to the lawsuit filed Monday.

The complaint, which named President Trump alongside White House communications director Steven Cheung and chief of staff Susie Wiles, argues new White House policy surrounding press access “deprives the public of the reporting of those organizations, and it inevitably deprives them of the independent reporting of other news organizations as well.”

“Every journalist who reports from the White House must now account for the possibility that a critical or ill-advised word about the president may result in their access being summarily restricted or revoked,” the lawsuit continued.

The 26-page filing asserted that the “threat of being targeted in the future is likely to distort the reporting of news organizations today,” adding that “protecting the public’s right to independent reporting requires broader equitable relief.”

The lawsuit asked the courts to “adequately protect the right to receive independent White House reporting” and declare the White House’s policy “unconstitutional because it imposes restrictions on a limited public forum that are viewpoint-based and unreasonable.”

A White House official told The Hill: “No person may demand access to the Oval Office.”

“Media that pedal misinformation and defamation are completely capable of reporting their manufactured stories from directly outside,” the official added.

“The White House cannot decide what information Americans receive by punishing critical reporting,” Katie Fallow, the deputy litigation director at Knight First Amendment Institute, one of the organizations that filed the lawsuit on behalf of the six plaintiffs, said in a press release .

“When the White House expels reporters because of their coverage and threatens others with expulsion, it isn’t just the press that suffers—the public loses access to independent reporting and gets something closer to government propaganda,” Fallow continued.

The lawsuit references multiple attempts by the Trump administration to restrict press access to the White House and the Pentagon, including the decision to bar Politico, CNN and MS NOW from the White House in September.

A federal judge issued a block on Trump’s ban of the three major news organizations, ruling the outlets were likely not given enough due process.

The Independent’s Andrew Feinberg recently reported that he was removed from his print press pool duties by the White House after the president lashed out at the reporter in the Oval Office.

Feinberg along with some CNN reporters have also stated they were still unable to join the press pool on Air Force One.

articles.title: Vance, Harris top early 2028 White House race polling
articles.summary: Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are at the top of early polling for the GOP presidential nod in 2028, while former Vice President Kamala Harris leads a wide-open Democratic field. A New York Times/Siena University survey released last week found Vance with 33 percent support from Republican primary voters, 10 points…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are at the top of early polling for the GOP presidential nod in 2028, while former Vice President Kamala Harris leads a wide-open Democratic field.

A New York Times/Siena University survey released last week found Vance with 33 percent support from Republican primary voters, 10 points ahead of Rubio.

President Trump has repeatedly floated both men as potential contenders, though Vance, long seen as the heir apparent, has said he’s never spoken to the president about running, and Rubio has said he’s not planning to mount a bid next cycle.

Trump, who in the past has floated running for an unconstitutional third term, snagged 8 percent, signaling his lasting grip on the GOP as he heads into the last half of his second term.

Trump was followed by Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R), who challenged Trump in 2024, at 3 percent. Another 6 percent of Republican respondents named someone else, and 26 percent said they didn’t know who to back.

Across the aisle, Harris snagged 12 percent support from Democratic primary voters, ahead of California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) with 9 percent and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg with 7 percent.

Progressive Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) and Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) also pulled in single-digit support, with 6 percent, 4 percent and 3 percent, respectively.

But another 15 percent in the party named other candidates — and a whopping 45 percent said they didn’t know who they’d pick for the next White House race.

Roughly half of Democratic respondents said they want to see their party move toward the center as 2028 approaches, compared with 27 percent who said it should shift left and 21 percent who said it should stay as is. A staggering 72 percent of the pivotal independent bloc, though, also said the Democrats should move toward the center.

More than 80 percent of independents also said they want Republicans to move away from Trump, though just a third of Republicans said the same.

The survey was conducted Oct. 12-19 among 3,494 voters. The margin of sampling error was 1.9 percentage points among the likely electorate and registered voters.

articles.title: US midterm elections 2026 in maps and charts
articles.summary: On November 3, Americans decide which party controls the US Congress for the second half of Donald Trump’s presidency.
articles.body:
On November 3, about 210 million registered voters will decide how much power Donald Trump has for the rest of his US presidency.

Trump is not on the ballot, but control of the United States Congress is. Made up of the House of Representatives and the Senate, Congress writes the country’s laws and controls federal spending.

In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera breaks down how the elections work, which races matter and what the results could mean for either party.

Held halfway through a US president’s four-year term, midterm elections decide the makeup of Congress.

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats are being contested, including special elections in the states of Florida and Ohio to fill the seats vacated by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance. Voters in 36 states will also elect governors.

House members represent one congressional district each and serve two-year terms, while senators serve six-year terms.

Midterm elections are also widely considered a referendum on the sitting president’s performance.

Since 1946, the president’s party has lost an average of 26.5 seats in the House and a handful in the Senate in midterm elections, according to Todd Belt, a professor of political management at George Washington University.

Beyond Congress and governors, voters will also elect state legislators and local officials.

Nadia Brown, a professor of government at Georgetown University, said that while national elections get most of the attention, “It is important to remember that local politics is where most Americans interact with government.”

She added that “It is the local propositions or referendums on ballots [that] will impact the everyday lives of people.”

What is at stake in the House and Senate?

Republicans hold majorities in both chambers. Losing either would give Democrats the power to block legislation and launch investigations into Trump’s administration.

Democrats need to gain three seats in the House and four in the Senate to take control. A 50-50 split in the Senate would leave Republicans in control, because Vance can cast tie-breaking votes.

Belt said a Democratic victory could significantly limit Trump’s ability to pursue his domestic agenda.

“If Democrats take one chamber, all non-government funding legislation will grind to a halt,” he told Al Jazeera.

The House of Representatives is the lower house of the US Congress.

Its 435 members each represent one local district and serve two-year terms, so every seat is contested every two years.

Seats are divided among the states by population, based on the US Census conducted every 10 years. California, the most populous state, has 52 seats, while the least populous, such as Wyoming and Vermont, have one each.

Republicans currently control the House, with 218 seats to the Democrats’ 214, and one independent sits with the Republicans. Two seats are vacant, one last held by each party.

The new House will be sworn in on January 3, 2027.

Each district elects its own representative, and the party that wins 218 seats takes control, so a few narrow wins in close districts can decide the majority.

Belt estimates that about 35 House races could decide the majority. He predicts Democrats could gain about 15 seats, despite Republican redistricting that he says has given the party an advantage in nine additional districts.

“People generally vote straight ticket, meaning they will vote for all the candidates of one party, so this is likely to affect down-ballot races [as well],” he said.

A battleground district is a seat either party could realistically win. The graphic below highlights 12 of these key races to watch.

The Senate is the upper house of the US Congress.

Its 100 members, two from each state regardless of population, are elected statewide and serve six-year terms, with about a third of seats contested every two years.

This year, 33 seats are being contested in regular elections, alongside special elections in Florida and Ohio. Those two contests will fill the remaining two years of terms previously held by Marco Rubio and JD Vance.

Of the 35 seats being contested, Republicans hold 22, and Democrats hold 13.

Republicans currently have 53 senators. Democrats have 45, and two independents sit with them, giving the Democratic bloc 47 seats.

Democrats need a net gain of four seats to reach 51 and take control. Republicans can keep control with 50 because Vice President Vance can break tied votes.

The new Senate will be sworn in on January 3, 2027.

To win the Senate, Democrats must hold the 13 seats they are defending and flip Republican-held ones.

In Georgia, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff faces Republican Mike Collins. Michigan’s open seat pits Democrat Abdul El-Sayed against Republican Mike Rogers, while Democrat Chris Pappas faces Republican John Sununu for an open seat in New Hampshire.

Republican-held seats offer Democrats opportunities elsewhere. In Maine, Senator Susan Collins faces Democrat Troy Jackson, who replaced primary winner Graham Platner after he withdrew in July. North Carolina’s open seat pits Democrat Roy Cooper against Republican Michael Whatley.

Ohio, Alaska and Iowa are also competitive, while Texas and Kansas have drawn growing attention as Democrats look for more routes to a majority.

Although Democrats face a more difficult path to a Senate majority than to control of the House, the growing number of competitive races has increased their chances of winning the chamber, according to election analysts.

The cost of living tops voters’ concerns, with rising petrol prices, housing costs and healthcare coverage squeezing household budgets.

Reproductive rights remain a major issue, while immigration and the state of US democracy are also on the ballot.

The US-Israel war on Iran and the rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI)` and data centres have raised further questions about security, jobs and energy costs.

About 210 million Americans are registered to vote, nearly eight in 10 US residents aged 18 or older, according to USAFacts, a nonpartisan organisation that compiles government data.

California has the most registered voters, with 23.2 million, followed by Texas (17.4 million) and Florida (13.6 million). Together, they account for about 26 percent of all registered voters.

Wyoming (278,468), Vermont (459,455) and Alaska (603,310) have the fewest.

A Pew Research Center survey conducted from September 28 to October 4 found that 44 percent of registered voters backed the Democratic candidate in their district, compared with 36 percent for the Republican. Five percent support another candidate, and 15 percent are unsure.

Men are evenly split, with 42 percent backing each party, while women favour Democrats by 45 percent to 31 percent.

The graphic below shows how voting preferences differ by gender, race, age, education and party affiliation.

Fewer Americans vote in midterms than in presidential elections. Since 1944, average turnout has been about 42 percent in midterms, compared with 58 percent in presidential races.

What happens if Republicans lose the House?

A Democratic House could block Republican legislation and use its committees to investigate the Trump administration. It would also hold the power to impeach the president, which only the House can do.

Control would also give Democrats leverage over government funding. Every bill needs approval from both chambers, so a Republican Senate could not pass laws on its own.

Belt expects a Democratic-controlled House to lead to more confrontations over federal spending, including the 12 annual bills needed to fund federal agencies. That raises the possibility of further government shutdowns, when funding lapses and many federal services stop.

Belt also believes that Trump could turn increasingly to foreign policy if his domestic agenda faces opposition in Congress.

“Traditionally, presidents facing divided government in their last two years pivot to foreign policy almost exclusively. I think the same will be true for Trump,” he said.

What happens if Republicans lose the Senate?

A Democratic Senate could block legislation and reject presidential nominees, including federal judges, Supreme Court justices, cabinet officials and ambassadors.

That makes Senate control consequential beyond the next two years. Federal judges serve for life, shaping rulings long after a presidency ends.

The Senate also holds the trial if the House impeaches a president. Removing a president from office requires a two-thirds majority, a threshold neither party is likely to reach.

Would winning both chambers give Democrats full control?

No. Trump would remain president and could veto legislation, and overriding a veto requires a two-thirds vote in each chamber.

Senate rules also require 60 votes to end debate on most legislation, though some budget bills can pass with a simple majority. A narrow majority therefore does not guarantee a party can pass its programme.

A Democratic House could open impeachment proceedings against Trump, who has already been impeached twice. However, removing a president from office requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate.

Belt considers another impeachment unlikely.

“There will definitely be investigations,” he told Al Jazeera, but added, “There will not likely be another impeachment because Democrats tried that twice and Republicans rallied behind Trump.”

Results will begin emerging after the first polls close at 6pm Eastern time (23:00 GMT) on November 3, but some close races could take days to resolve.

Election night results are preliminary. Final tallies can take days or sometimes weeks as officials count mail-in, provisional and other outstanding ballots before certifying the results, and the pace varies by state.

“In some states, it may take up to a week or more,” Belt said.

Some contests may go further. In Georgia, if no Senate candidate wins a majority, the race goes to a run-off election on December 1.

Belt warned that early results could give a misleading picture of the outcome. Because Republicans have historically been less likely than Democrats to vote by mail, some states could initially appear to favour Republican candidates before later-counted ballots narrow or reverse their leads. This is known as the “red mirage”. In states that count mail ballots first, the reverse can happen.

A delay in counting or a change in which candidate is leading does not, by itself, indicate electoral fraud.

The vote will decide who writes legislation, scrutinises the administration and controls federal spending, setting the balance of power for the rest of Trump’s term.

articles.title: Trump faces private citizens lawsuit over limiting White House media access
articles.summary: The plaintiffs argue they are losing access to vital information media outlets covering Trump used to provide.
articles.body:
A group of private citizens has sued the administration of United States President Donald Trump over its restrictions on news outlets covering the White House.

“All of the Plaintiffs rely on the White House press corps for independent reporting about the president and his administration, and all of them use that reporting in a variety of ways in their scholarship, teaching, journalism, or advocacy,” says the lawsuit, filed on Monday in a federal court in New York.

The lawsuit is the first lodged not by the news outlets being banned, but by those who consume the news and rely on it for their work.

The plaintiffs include a human rights advocate, a media watchdog, a university history professor, a high school teacher, a legal journalist and a student journalist.

Each argues they need unbiased, diverse media reporting from the White House to do their work.

“I’m gravely concerned that the Trump administration’s restrictions on White House reporters are cutting off access to crucial information,” Peter Schmidt-Nowara, a high school social studies teacher in New York City, said in a statement.

“I joined this lawsuit because my students deserve to know what’s happening in their government and to hear from a free and independent press.”

Trump already faces several legal challenges to his practice of banning journalists from outlets he dislikes from accessing the White House.

Last month, he banned journalists from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from attending news conferences at the White House. A federal judge later ruled the order was unconstitutional, a violation of the First Amendment, which protects freedom of the press, and ordered access be restored. However, the Trump administration continues to fight the ruling.

Last week, Trump dismissed reporting that he planned to evict journalists from the White House press briefing room and restore a swimming pool that was housed there starting in 1933. But he said he is still considering moving the press out of the briefing room.

“I am thinking about moving the Press, and putting them in a different location, but I will use that location for very badly needed space,” Trump said in a social media post.

Kenneth Roth, a senior fellow at Yale University and former executive director of Human Rights Watch, said the restrictions on press access were familiar postmarks in countries whose leaders have become authoritarian.

“Worldwide, I have seen how governmental leaders’ efforts to penalise independent journalists are a prelude to the rise of autocracy,” he said in a statement.

articles.title: Dollar General is sued by the FTC and 20 states for what's being described as deceptive pricing
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — The Federal Trade Commission has sued the bargain chain Dollar General for what it characterized as “long-running deceptive pricing practices...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — The Federal Trade Commission has sued the bargain chain Dollar General for what it characterized as "long-running deceptive pricing practices" by charging customers more once they reach the register than the prices that are displayed on shelves and in advertisements.

Twenty states joined in the complaint, filed by the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee. It said that Dollar General failed to correct the issue despite what it said was "extensive corporate knowledge of the problem."

"Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last," wrote Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection.

Dollar General, based in Goodlettsville, Tennessee, just outside of Nashville, did not immediately return a request for comment from The Associated Press.

The states joining the FTC lawsuit include: Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin, according to the FTC.

Americans have become frustrated with higher prices, and also what they perceive to be new methods used by restaurant chains and major retailers in setting prices including the use of artificial intelligence tools.

articles.title: Obama judge rules Trump DOJ illegally fired James Comey's daughter, rejects sweeping Article II claim
articles.summary: The Trump Justice Department fired Maurene Comey without cause, but a federal judge ruled it violated the Civil Service Reform Act and ordered backpay.
articles.body: An Obama-appointed New York federal judge ruled Monday that the Trump Justice Department unlawfully fired former FBI Director James Comey's daughter Maurene, rejecting the administration's sweeping claim of executive authority and warning that its argument threatened the nation's constitutional balance of power. The Justice Department acknowledged in court filings that Comey's firing was not for-cause and was not based on her performance, but argued that the attorney general had the authority to remove her under Article II of the Constitution. "Defendants’ argument that [Constitution] Article II bars Congress from regulating the removal of AUSAs (assistant U.S. attorneys) flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent," Judge Jesse Furman wrote, adding that accepting the administration's argument would "unsettle the very equilibrium established by this nation's constitutional system." TRUMP’S FIRING POWER FACES TWIN SUPREME COURT TESTS, BUT ONE AGENCY MAY GET SPECIAL TREATMENT A DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital the department disagreed with the decision and will appeal it in "due course." Furman ordered Comey retroactively reinstated and awarded back pay through Dec. 20, 2025, when she accepted another job. While federal law gives the attorney general authority to fire assistant U.S. attorneys, Furman ruled that Congress placed limits on that power through the Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA), which generally requires cause for termination and procedural protections for government workers. OBAMA JUDGE HALTS TRUMP FIRING BID AS DECADES-OLD LEGAL AUTHORITY TEES UP POSSIBLE MAJOR REVERSAL The judge found that Comey's firing violated those requirements, noting that the government conceded her removal was not based on misconduct or poor performance and that she received neither advance notice nor an opportunity to respond. Comey had served about a decade in the prominent Southern District of New York, where she worked on some of the office’s biggest cases, including the prosecution of Ghislaine Maxwell – associate and rumored partner of Jeffrey Epstein — as well as the sex trafficking trial of rapper Sean "P. Diddy" Combs. Furman also recently rebuked the Trump administration during its efforts to deport pro-Palestinian Columbia University student activist Mahmoud Khalil, leading the federal government to argue for a change of venue to New Jersey. The judge, nominated in 2011, previously served as a federal prosecutor in the same Manhattan U.S. attorney's office where both Comeys worked during their careers. Furman's brother, Jason, served in the Obama administration as chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers. James Comey served as the top prosecutor at SDNY early in the George W. Bush administration, where he investigated President Bill Clinton’s controversial pardon of financier Marc Rich as well as interior designer Martha Stewart. The younger Comey was the second in her family to be fired under Trump, after the president terminated her father as FBI director in 2017 during the Russia collusion investigation. The elder Comey later came under fire for posting a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to form the sentiment "86 47" – with critics saying "86" was a reference to killing something, such as in restaurant lingo, and "47" referred to Trump, the 47th president. Maurene Comey’s attorneys said in a statement to The Associated Press that their victory was "hard-earned" for both their client and all civil servants. articles.title: Haley Stevens ripped by fellow Dems for refusing to explicitly back El-Sayed: 'Stay the f--- off television'
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed's former primary rival Haley Stevens dodged a direct endorsement on CNN's "State of the Union," sparking progressive backlash online.
articles.body: Abdul El-Sayed's former Democratic rival is getting hammered by fellow left-wingers online for failing to explicitly endorse him during a weekend television appearance. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., who unsuccessfully ran for the Democratic nomination for Senate in Michigan, told CNN's "State of the Union" that she broadly supports her state party's ticket for the coming midterm elections. "Look, I'm on the Democratic ticket. I can't say that I agree with everything that's gone on," Stevens answered. "I'm looking to be on the team to support my next governor, Jocelyn Benson, and frankly, these great Democrats who are working their tails off, who are going to make Hakeem Jeffries the first Black Speaker of the House." BERNIE SANDERS CLAIMS SOME DEMOCRATS MAY WANT THEIR OWN SENATE NOMINEE TO LOSE When pressed about El-Sayed specifically, she said, "Well, look, I would just say, if you had asked me if I'm still on the team, I'm on the team." But that was not enough for progressives, who promptly accused Stevens of undermining her fellow Democrat. "Ridiculous. For all the folks still pretending El-Sayed’s race is the same as [Roy Cooper’s] or [Mary Peltola’s], do they have former Dem rivals refusing to fully endorse them on national TV? ‘Blue no matter who’ was a hypocritical centrist lie and this hypocrisy may hurt Dems in 2028," Mehdi Hasan wrote on X, referring to Democrat Senate races in North Carolina and Alaska. Leah Greenberg, who leads the progressive activist group Indivisible, wrote, "It is late October and people are voting every day, if you cannot give a full-throated endorsement to the Democratic nominee who could be the key vote in flipping the Senate, then stay the f--- off television." MICHIGAN DEMOCRAT WHO LOST SENATE PRIMARY TO ABDUL EL-SAYED TAKES AIM AT BERNIE SANDERS OVER ISRAEL STANCE Former congressional candidate Kyle Blomquist accused Stevens of "practically fawning over Mike Rogers" and said "her only real ideological commitment is to zionism." Progressive commentator Emma Vigeland wrote on X, "There are financial and institutional incentives to remain on the side of genocide. Stevens is sabotaging El-Sayed on national TV, one week before the midterm, to protect her pocketbook and career over democracy." More moderate and establishment-friendly Democrats pushed back on some of the criticism. Strategist Lis Smith responded to Hasan, "People—Democrats, Republicans, Independents—clamoring to support the Peltolas and Coopers is actually a validation of their candidate quality! It’s good to have candidates people want to associate with and that should be a factor when assessing candidate quality!" El-Sayed edged Stevens out by just 1% in the Michigan primary earlier this year, after fellow Democrat Mallory McMorrow dropped out of the race. El-Sayed won 48.5% of the vote compared to Stevens' 47.5%, with McMorrow netting 4%. Stevens was notably the establishment-backed pick with support from top Democrats like Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. El-Sayed is backed by "Squad" Democrats like Reps. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. articles.title: Somali rap promising to 'scatter' enemies underscores Omar's serene lakeside video
articles.summary: Ilhan Omar's lakeside video featured a Somali hip-hop song with lyrics about enemies scattering, posted days after HSI agents raided her D.C. home.
articles.body: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., posted a serene lakeside video Friday set to a Somali hip-hop song whose lyrics boast of enemies scattering and being "crushed," days after federal agents searched her Washington home as part of a criminal investigation. "Less scrolling, more strolling. Enjoying our beautiful Minnesota lakes," the embattled congresswoman wrote on X in a post made at the end of last week. She attached a video of herself and her husband, Tim Mynett, walking on a dock over a lake with vibrant fall foliage in the background. The pair posed, smiled and appeared to chat as they serenely strolled across the dock, looking fondly at each other as the lawmaker running for reelection held a coffee. It ended with a montage of images from their walk. But a loud Somali hip-hop song accompanying the video told a much different story. ILHAN OMAR DOUBLES DOWN ON ‘REAL NAME’ WHEN CONFRONTED AT MALL OF SOMALIA "Let me reveal who I really am. No enemy dares threaten me, wherever I step, they scatter," the lyrics to the song say in Somali, according to a translation obtained by Fox News Digital. "They flee and stay far away. I have always been the source of their distress." The song, "Nimaan Ciilayba Icaaya," is by Ilkacase Qays, whose real name is Muse Abdikadir. His website describes him as a "U.S. based Somali singer, rapper and activist." The duet-style track features Somali singer Hodan Abdirahman. A cultural analysis of the song says it is "a powerful example of Somali lyrical poetry built around pride, bravery, personal dignity and unwavering trust in Allah." "A fool’s words carry no weight," the lyrics say. "Those I have angered now insult me. If the just one had felt anger on my behalf, would he not have crushed the enemy underfoot? With the strength the almighty has given me, If I draw on it late in the afternoon, by evening, I will have taught you a lesson." FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION The analysis describes the artist as using "exaggerated imagery to ridicule his opponents, portraying them as people who would lose sleep, suffer humiliation, and even seek supernatural assistance out of desperation." "You go without sleep, overcome with anguish, weeping in spite," the lyrics continued. "You howl like a demon through the night, because you cannot match me! Swallow your anger and choke on it if the just one had felt anger on my behalf." Omar, who sources say is actually named Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, reemerged in Minnesota on Friday. It came after nearly two weeks out of the public eye following an Oct. 12, 2026, raid on her Washington, D.C., home, conducted by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents. Members of the media followed her intently as she cast an early ballot alongside state Attorney General Keith Ellison at a polling place in Minneapolis on Friday. The pair then appeared at the Karmel Mall of Somalia in Minneapolis, where they enjoyed lunch among members of the Somali community and posed for photographs. HOMAN SAYS ILHAN OMAR COULD BE STRIPPED OF NATURALIZATION, DEPORTED IF IMMIGRATION FRAUD IS PROVEN Later in the day, Omar posted the video to X. It is unclear when it was filmed. The Somali-born Minnesota lawmaker restricted who can respond directly to her social media post, with the only publicly facing comment being from ousted former U.S. House "Squad" member Cori Bush, who wrote: "We love this." Omar is being investigated for potential fraud related to immigration paperwork filled out by her or her father when she was becoming a United States citizen. HSI is the main investigatory agency for the Department of Homeland Security. During the raid, Omar's passport and cellphone were confiscated by federal agents. Her sister, Sahra Noor, was interviewed by federal investigators in the wake of the raid. Federal agents have also obtained Omar's DNA, Fox News reported. articles.title: Nate Silver: Polling ‘would have to be very wrong’ for Republicans to maintain House control
articles.summary: Pollster Nate Silver claimed Sunday that polling “would have to be very wrong” for Republicans to hold on to the House, comments that came a little more than a week before this year’s midterms. “You’ve seen high turnout in Democratic primaries all year. We talk about the early voting data too. You know, the hard…
articles.body:
Pollster Nate Silver claimed Sunday that polling “ would have to be very wrong ” for Republicans to hold on to the House, comments that came a little more than a week before this year’s midterms.

“You’ve seen high turnout in Democratic primaries all year. We talk about the early voting data too. You know, the hard place versus the rock, I guess, is that, to win the Senate, Democrats have to win in some states that President Trump carried by double digits in 2024,” Silver told CNN’s Fareed Zakaria on his show.

“So, that’s why in the House, the polling would have to be very wrong, more wrong than 2016 for Democrats to fail to win the House, but the Senate, everyone’s trying to guess: Will this wave be big enough to inundate red states like Texas, Iowa, Ohio, Kansas, Alaska?”

Republicans are facing an uphill battle with Election Day almost a week away. The party is facing issues like the unpopular war in Iran, concerns about the cost of living and Trump’s slumping approval rating.

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 39.3 percent Monday afternoon, and his disapproval rating was at 59.3 percent.

DDHQ also forecast that the Democrats will garner 235 House seats in this year’s midterms, 17 seats more than the 218 needed for the House majority .

When it comes to the Senate, DDHQ has also forecast that the Democrats will garner 51 seats in the upcoming elections, gaining the majority in the chamber as well.

Energy costs have become central to this year’s midterms, with the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the oil industry, closed amid the conflict with Iran. Recent polls have shown that voters blame the Trump administration for higher prices, further complicating the Republicans’ midterm landscape.

On Monday afternoon, the average price of a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. was about $4.29, up from about $3.05 last year at the same time, according to AAA.

images.caption: Nate Silver speaks at “On The Fault Lines: Decision 2018” Midterm Election Panel on Oct. 25, 2018, in New York City.

articles.title: Man charged with mailing threatening letters with white substance to members of Congress
articles.summary: A man has been charged in Illinois with mailing four letters containing a white granular substance to members of Congress, all of which were sent in envelopes containing his name and home address.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — A man has been charged in Illinois with mailing four letters containing a white granular substance to members of Congress, all of which were sent in envelopes containing his name and home address. Matthew Unglesbee has been charged with sending threatening letters containing a white granular substance to three members of Congress, along with a handwritten letter that read “HA HA.” A fourth letter with a white granular substance included the note “HAH enjoy the gift.” Unglesbee is facing two charges: false information and hoaxes, and mailing threatening communications. He will make an initial appearance in court on Monday afternoon. In an interview with FBI personnel on Sunday, Unglesbee allegedly admitted that he mailed four letters to four members of Congress after hearing about other letters mailed earlier in the month. The FBI is separately investigating letters containing suspicious substances that were sent to members of Congress and elections officials in recent weeks. Unglesbee admitted that he knew that people would perceive the letters as dangerous, the FBI says. He said in the FBI interview that the granular substance was salt, which he said “kind of looks like” anthrax. He denied involvement with prior mailings. A search of his residence turned up a fifth unmailed and empty envelope that was addressed to a member of Congress, according to the FBI. The case began after an anonymous online tipster told the FBI that they overheard Unglesbee talking about mailing a suspicious substance to members of Congress. The tip was received on Oct. 16, and the FBI responded when the letters showed up to the offices of members of Congress three days later.
