articles.title: ‘Deflections’: Abdul El-Sayed responds to Trump’s anti-Muslim attacks
articles.summary: The Democratic candidate for the US Senate has been the subject of Islamophobic attacks from Trump.
articles.body:
Detroit, Michigan – Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed has dismissed United States President Donald Trump’s anti-Muslim attacks against him, saying that they are an attempt to move the attention away from the president’s own record.

At a news conference in Detroit on Monday, El-Sayed said Trump is trying to distract from issues that matter to Americans – including petrol prices and the war on Iran – by accusing the Democratic candidate of being a “jihadist”.

El-Sayed called the attacks “deflections and deceptions based on no evidence”.

“They have nothing to say about solving the problems in your life. They’re not talking about you,” the Democratic candidate said of Republicans.

“They’re not talking about your gas or your groceries … They’re not talking about clean air or clean water. They’re not talking about any of the things that the government is actually supposed to solve. Why? Because Donald Trump has created those problems.”

At a rally in Michigan on Sunday, Trump unleashed repeated baseless claims against El-Sayed, accusing the Democrat of wanting to impose “Sharia law” on the country.

“He would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate,” Trump said. “I want him to have a metal detector.”

El-Sayed laughed off the suggestion that he may personally be a physical threat to Congress. “He knows I got those Wolverine claws,” he said, a reference to the sports teams of his alma mater, the University of Michigan.

The progressive Democrat and former public health official is locked in a close race with former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers, a contest that could decide the Senate majority for the next two years.

Rogers has made unfounded allegations linking El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, Hamas and Hezbollah a central point of his campaign.

On Monday, El-Sayed said most Americans reject such attacks.

“There are always a few small people who want to make America small like that. You see them; they’re very loud, and they bark,” El-Sayed said.

“The vast majority of folks in this state believe in a big America. They’re open-minded. They’re big-hearted. And the story of America is those who believe in big America, overcoming the deception, the distraction, the sad attempts of the small-minded to make us small.”

He added that “Michiganders are a lot bigger than that”.

El-Sayed also addressed Trump’s statements mocking his name and misrepresenting it as “Mohamed”.

“My name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your gas – not the reason you can’t afford your groceries, not the reason you can’t pay your rent, your mortgage, not the reason you can’t see a doctor,” he said.

images.caption: Michigan Democrat senatorial candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at a midterm campaign rally in Grand Rapids, Michigan, on October 25, 2026 [Jeff Kowalsky/AFP]

articles.title: Texas redistricting left these Latino voters confused, but will it impact midterm vote?
articles.summary: The electoral map that Texas redrew at President Donald Trump’s request left many voters in Houston and southern Texas facing unfamiliar candidates.
articles.body: HOUSTON — When José Cantú checked his voter registration information one morning in early October, he discovered that his house was no longer in Texas’s 29th Congressional District, which Democratic Congresswoman Sylvia García represents. Two years ago, when he voted for the first time, Cantú cast a ballot for García, whom he says he’s known since he was “a little boy.” Now, “I texted my mom and said, ‘Mom, we’re now part of District 9. What am I going to do?’” said Cantú, a medical student at the University of Houston, referring to the fact that he didn’t recognize anyone listed on the ballot and had to figure out who the candidates were. Although Cantú, 20, didn’t move, the map of his district had changed. His friend, Jessica Campos, 44, a mother of three, was also unaware of the changes and believed she still voted in District 29, not District 9. “I didn’t know until a few days ago who our candidate was,” she said. “Even though I’m very interested in politics, I didn’t know who was representing me.” Cantú and Campos are not isolated cases. In 2025, at the request of President Donald Trump, the Texas Legislature redrew its electoral map with the aim of taking away five congressional seats from Democrats who represented a Latino- or Black majority-district. Texas thus opened a redistricting race that extended to a dozen states, from California to Florida. Districts 9 and 34 show what this change means for many Latino voters. In Houston’s newly created District 9, 97 out of every 100 residents were in a different district in the 2024 election; in the case of District 34, in the southern part of the state, the map swapped areas near McAllen with Corpus Christi. Both districts have a Hispanic majority and, according to experts, both were drawn to favor a Republican candidate. According to analysts, the Republican strategy for the new electoral map rests on two assumptions: that many Latinos don’t vote and that those who voted for President Donald Trump in 2024 will vote Republican again. On Nov. 3, with control of the House of Representatives at stake, it will become clear whether this was a sound gamble. But first, nearly all residents of the new 9th District and more than a third of those in the 34th District, which is also a new district, will have to figure out who the candidates on their ballots are. Most people unaware their district has changed “Our studies show that most people don’t know they’re in a new district,” said Mark P. Jones, a political scientist at Rice University. Republicans have made no secret of their intentions in pushing for the new maps. “The underlying goal of this plan is simple: to improve Republican political performance,” state representative Todd Hunter, a Corpus Christi Republican who introduced the map in the House, said in August of 2025. Hunter emphasized that four of the five new districts have a Hispanic majority. This electoral practice, known as gerrymandering, involves drawing districts to give an advantage to a particular party or group. In November 2025, a federal court ruled 2-1 that Texas’ gerrymandering was racial-based: the map was drawn using voters’ race as the primary criterion, which violates the Constitution. Texas countered that its motive was partisan, not racial, and asked the Supreme Court to block the federal ruling. The Supreme Court ultimately allowed the state to use its new maps. “We thought the 2021 map was a problem, but the 2025 map made it much worse,” said Thomas Saenz, president of the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund (MALDEF), which is litigating against both maps. According to Saenz, the new redrawing eliminated effective Latino majorities in several districts. The lawsuit remains open and, he said, will be resolved after the election. In response to a request for comment from Noticias Telemundo, Eduardo Leal, campaign spokesperson for Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, said the maps “were drawn to comply with the law.” Same number, new district The old District 9, in southwest Houston, united Black and Latino voters; Kamala Harris won it by 44 points in 2004 and veteran Democrat Al Green had represented it since 2005. When the new map drew much of that territory into District 18, Green followed suit and in May lost the Democratic primary runoff to Christian Menefee. The new District 9 retains its number and almost nothing else. Only 3% of its residents lived in the old district: the rest came from the former Districts 29, 36 and 2, according to an analysis by Jones and Michael O. Adams of Texas Southern University. The new boundaries encompass eastern Harris County, including the East End, the Houston Canal corridor and all of rural, predominantly white Liberty County. Had this been the case two years ago, Trump would have won it by 20 points. On paper, District 9 is a Latino district: 62% of its residents are Hispanic. But only about 50% are eligible to vote due to age and citizenship status, and only 45% are registered voters. In 2024, Latinos accounted for only 37% of TX-9 voters, according to Jones’ and Adams’ analysis. “Although it has a Latino majority, it’s a district where the majority of voters are white,” Jones said. Districts are drawn using the total population, including minors and noncitizens, and the designers “know that within that Latino district there’s a low percentage who are actually going to turn out to vote,” he explained. Liberty County, a rural area that accounts for just under a fifth of the district’s voters, tips the scales in favor of Republicans. There, Republican Alex Mealer leads Democrat Leticia Gutierrez by 37 points, while on Harris’ side it’s a virtual tie, according to a University of Houston Hobby School poll co-authored by Jones. Ryan Taylor, chairman of the Republican Party in Liberty, said that the new district gives its voters a more important role. “It would be a mistake to assume that a voter’s ethnicity determines their political priorities,” he said. For many voters, confusion For Jones, the biggest effect of the map is confusion. In Houston, many people no longer know who their representative is, he said, and with the second redistricting in a decade (the first was in 2021, after the 2020 census), “many are going to realize” when they go to vote. Leticia Gutierrez, the Democratic candidate in District 9, says she’s noticed confusion at her campaign events because some voters believe she’s running against Rep. Sylvia Garcia, also a Democrat. “They’re confusing them, and it’s on purpose,” she said. Daron Shaw, a professor of government at the University of Texas at Austin, says the strongest argument against redrawing the maps mid-decade is the confusion it creates because voters “don’t really know who their representative is,” and that damages the quality of representation. However, he added, “This isn’t new. Parties that control legislatures will almost always redraw districts in their favor.” Campos, the voter from District 9, sums it up like this: “It’s not fair that we don’t know who wants to represent us.” In July, an ICE agent shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Magnolia Park, an East End neighborhood that falls within the new district. His death shocked the Hispanic community in Texas and has prompted voters with a low propensity to participate to express their desire to vote to send a message to the Trump administration, according to local politicians and analysts. Gutierrez, District 9’s Democratic candidate, described Salgado Araujo as “a hard-working man who was employing people” and who “was simply going to his job.” Following his death, she said in a video posted to her Facebook account that the new District 9 layout was designed “to silence the East End.” Noticias Telemundo requested comment from candidate Alex Mealer’s team but had not received a response by the time of publication. The Republican candidate said in July that she trusted the investigations into Salgado’s death would provide “a full account” of what happened and that speculation “is neither helpful nor productive.” A district with two heads In South Texas, the map followed a different logic. District 34 lost its portion of Hidalgo County, near McAllen, and gained most of Nueces County, including Corpus Christi, which had belonged to the Republican 27th District. In 2024, with the previous boundaries, Trump won the district by 4.5 points, but the same voters re-elected Democrat Vicente Gonzalez as their representative. With the new boundaries, the district is now 77% Hispanic, and Trump would have won it by 10 points in 2024. As Jones explains, “it is now a district with two heads,” Brownsville to the south and more Democratic, and Corpus Christi to the north and more Republican. “They did this to try to get me out of Congress,” Vicente Gonzalez, the Democratic congressman running for re-election in that district, said. “What they didn’t count on is that I’m from Corpus Christi. That’s the community where I was born and raised.” Gonzalez estimates that, with the changes, he lost about 250,000 voters. With the changes, Hidalgo County was completely removed from District 34, and its eastern part was moved to District 15, according to Richard Gonzalez, chairman of the Democratic Party in that county. He fears that many voters may not know that these changes have already taken place. “Some may think they are voting for Vicente Gonzalez when in reality they are now voting for Bobby Pulido (Democratic candidate of the 15th),” he stated. An August poll by Texas Southern University gave Gonzalez a 2-point lead over Republican Eric Flores, within the margin of error. Among Latino voters alone, Gonzalez led 53 to 34; white voters favored Flores 57 to 31. Noticias Telemundo requested comments from Flores’ team but, at the time of publication, had not received a response. Flores, a former federal prosecutor in McAllen and former National Guard captain, has the backing of both Trump and Abbott. “South Texas needs a fighter, not an absentee congressman,” he said in May. On immigration, he has shown nuance: in 2025, he said he wants employers to “have the workers they need” through an efficient legal process. According to Jones, there are no radical candidates competing in this district: The candidates from both parties are centrist Latinos, and ultimately the election will be decided by “the centrist Latino who voted for Trump in 2024, but today has doubts.” ‘We have a lot of power’ Some analysts agree that the new Texas maps were drawn based on the results of the 2024 election, but they disagree on how much that will weigh on the November vote. “There is no evidence that Hispanics are becoming more Republican,” said Mike Madrid, a Republican political consultant and critic of Trump. His party, he said, “mistakenly believed” after 2024 that it had figured out Latinos. He said that, between that mistake and the political climate, the election is shaping up to be “an extraordinary fiasco” for Republicans. Jason Villalba, a former Republican legislator and founder of the Texas Hispanic Policy Foundation, called the new map “a blatant political maneuver” and believes the Legislature mistook an economic vote for a realignment. “Republicans are in for a big surprise on election night,” he asserted. Shaw, the University of Texas professor, estimates that Republicans have gone from having nearly 50% of the Latino vote in 2024 to perhaps 40% in current polls. He calculates that, in the best-case scenario, Republicans will win two or three of the five seats they were seeking. Meanwhile, Cantú, the medical student, said he wanted to organize workshops so other young people can learn about the changes in their districts and get to know the candidates. “It makes me angry because they don’t give us the correct information,” he said. For her part, Cantu’s friend Jessica Campos said that Hispanic voters have “a lot of power.” “The problem is,” she said, “we don’t know it yet.” An earlier version of this story was first featured in Noticias Telemundo.

articles.title: Bipartisan pair of former South Carolina governors endorse Andrews for Senate
articles.summary: A bipartisan pair of former South Carolina governors endorsed Democrat Annie Andrews over Sen. Darline Graham (R) in the state’s Senate election. Former South Carolina Govs. David Beasley (R) and Jim Hodges (D) appeared in a video for Andrews’s campaign on Monday. “Now, over the years, the two of us haven’t always agreed on everything,”…
articles.body:
A bipartisan pair of former South Carolina governors endorsed Democrat Annie Andrews over Sen. Darline Graham (R) in the state’s Senate election .

Former South Carolina Govs. David Beasley (R) and Jim Hodges (D) appeared in a video for Andrews’s campaign on Monday.

“Now, over the years, the two of us haven’t always agreed on everything,” Hodges said.

“But one thing we do agree on right now is this country is too divided, and the political rhetoric has gotten way, way out of hand,” Beasley stated.

“That is why we’re coming together today to support Annie Andrews,” Hodges continued.

“Annie understands that leadership isn’t about making people angrier. Well, it’s about making things better,” Beasley added. “Well, we may have served as your governor from different political parties, but we agree South Carolina deserves better than more of the same political fight.”

Hodges notably defeated Beasley in the 1998 South Carolina gubernatorial race and was the last Democrat to serve as the state’s governor.

Beasley has been critical of the Republican Party and its shift under President Trump. He wrote in an op-ed last week that this was “not the party that I knew, and it is not the party that I consider myself a member of.”

Andrews faces off against Graham, who was appointed to fill the seat belonging to her late brother, former Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). Darline Graham has relied on an endorsement from Trump to garner support, though the president faces growing dissatisfaction from voters over the war in Iran and rising cost of living.

During a candidate debate , Darline Graham was pressed on her ties to the president and his recent Russian oil deal, which supplies the U.S. and the global marketplace with 300,000 tons of diesel “immediately.”

She ultimately deferred to the president on the decision, saying, “It gives the president tools that he can use if he so chooses to end the war through economic sanctions. So that’s up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it or whether he wants to use something else.”

She then went on the offensive by attempting to tie Andrews to the Democratic Socialists of America.

“My opponent is going to stand up here tonight and call me a socialist because that’s what her script says,” Andrews said, “and also because she doesn’t want to talk to you about your high gas prices, grocery prices or your closing rural hospital.”

Cook Political Report, an election handicapper, shifted the race away from the GOP’s favor last week, citing a new wave of funding boosting Andrews’s chances in the election. Decision Desk HQ, The Hill’s partner, forecasted the race leaning in Graham’s favor, giving her a 67 percent chance of winning, while Andrews has a 33 percent chance.

articles.title: Brazilian election sends US progressives into online fever as key irregularity stokes result uncertainty
articles.summary: Lula's Brazil election victory sparked celebration from U.S. progressives like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, but a last-minute voting extension drew sharp criticism.
articles.body: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's victory securing a fourth term spurred a social media firestorm Monday morning as progressives in the United States celebrated his win from afar. "Yesterday, Brazil showed the world that the will of the people is stronger than the authoritarians who try to suppress it," Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., said in a post to X. "Congratulations, President [Lula] and congratulations Brazil." Progressives have framed Lula’s victory as a transnational repudiation of what they regard as the core politics of the Trump administration and its allies. But questions about the election remain after one of Brazil's Supreme Court justices granted a last-minute extension of the country's polling hours, prompting Lula's opponent to question the legitimacy of the outcome. In the waning hours of the election, Lula requested a two-hour extension of voting hours from the country’s Supreme Court, citing delayed public transportation services. Less than half an hour before the polls were scheduled to close, Supreme Court Justice Christiano Zanin granted the extension nationwide, prompting an outcry from Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula’s opponent. CONSERVATIVE WAVE HITS ROADBLOCK IN BRAZIL AS LULA HOLDS OFF BOLSONARO CHALLENGE "What happened today was not normal. It was something frankly unacceptable. A Supreme Court justice, for the first time in history — a former lawyer of Lula’s — issues an order at the request of a former partner of his and changes the rules of the game in the middle of the game," Bolsonaro said in a statement. Notably, Bolsonaro's campaign also asked for an extension, citing heavy rain. Election experts in the country, speaking with local media, said the inclement weather and polling extension could provide grounds for a legal challenge to the election. "There is the possibility of requesting the annulment of the election. The deluge that fell in Santa Catarina and Paraná caused harm. The lack of buses and the restriction of public transportation in strategic cities, such as Salvador and São Paulo, harmed the right to vote," Guilherme Gonçalves, an attorney and member of the Brazilian Academy of Electoral and Political Law, told Brazilian outlet GZH. Another expert, while casting doubt on whether a legal challenge would ultimately succeed, said uncertainty over the election would continue. "It is difficult for it to succeed, but the point is that the [Supreme Court] contributed to the instability of the electoral process, which is serious," Guilherme Barcelos, an attorney with a doctorate in constitutional law and specialization in electoral law, told GZH. "The election does not end today. That is the point." In the meantime, several Republican figures back in the U.S. blasted the outcome. Martin De Luca, an attorney representing some of President Donald Trump’s media groups, accused Lula of benefiting from his political connections to the Supreme Court. "Yesterday Brazil showed the world that if you are losing an election and you need to turn it around, you can call on your former lawyer turned judge to give you a lift and you’ll still be congratulated by all who share the cause," De Luca wrote. Donald Trump Jr. echoed De Luca's criticism in a reply to his post. "If a conservative government in Brazil did this, everyone in the mainstream press in America would lose their minds, but I guess they’re just choosing to be silent because it’s all for the cause," Trump Jr. said. BLANCHE WON'T RULE OUT DOJ BLOCKING ELECTION CERTIFICATION IN 'DOOMSDAY' SCENARIO "Brazil did not have an election today. They had their country stolen from them by a criminal band of corrupt hacks who belong in jail," Joey Mannarino, the co-founder of the Overton Institute, a conservative-leaning think tank, wrote. During his campaign, Bolsonaro built momentum on promises to increase public safety by expanding prison capacity and drastically cut the size of government through a 25% reduction in government ministries — policies that many Democrats viewed as mirroring efforts by the Trump administration. By contrast, Lula has advocated for anti-poverty programs, minimum-wage increases and expanded assistance for low-income families. The platform drew praise from progressive groups including the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). "It is with tremendous pride that the Democratic Socialists of America congratulate President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin … and the coalition of progressive and leftists parties on their victory and re-election in Brazil’s second round of presidential elections this past Sunday," the group wrote in a press release. TRUMP'S WAR ON DRUG CARTELS COULD GAIN POWERFUL NEW ALLY AFTER PIVOTAL ELECTION "We commend the wide range of forces that joined together … to defend Brazilian democracy and secure this victory." Other prominent progressives also celebrated Lula’s victory as a triumph for policies aligned with their own. "Lula has stood up for Brazilian workers and democracy — and will continue to do so in the next four years," Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., wrote in a post to X. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "People all across the world are fighting back against extremism. With Lula in Brazil, they just won," Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., said.

articles.title: Data center group jumps into the Kansas governor’s race to boost Republicans
articles.summary: Building the Future is an offshoot of the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future, arguably the leading super PAC promoting industry interests in the midterm elections.
articles.body: Building the Future, a new pro-data center super PAC, is spending more than $1.5 million to back Kansas state Sen. Ty Masterson, a Republican, in the state’s battle for governor, a person familiar with the spending said Monday in details first shared with NBC News. Building the Future is an offshoot of the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future, backed by AI heavyweights and arguably the leading super PAC promoting industry interests in the midterm elections. Earlier Monday, The New York Times reported that Building the Future is also set to spend about $1.5 million in advertising to boost GOP Sen. Darline Graham in the South Carolina Senate race. In August, Build American AI, a nonprofit that is also in the Leading the Future network, announced a multimillion-dollar ad campaign in Kansas, Ohio and Wisconsin seeking to boost preferred policies to govern data center growth. At the time, it announced the formation of the political group, Building the Future. The group said in August it would back candidates who support “responsible policies that strengthen and protect communities, preserve water resources, and prevent rate hikes on electricity bills, while ensuring American leadership in AI and creating good-paying jobs for American workers.” The new spending followed months of opposition to data center development intensifying, with the sprawling structures needed to power the AI boom becoming a key issue for voters across the country. Kansas is one of the only Democratic-controlled governorships that Republicans have a shot at flipping this fall. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report lists that race as leaning Republican. The state also features a competitive Senate contest between Republican Sen. Roger Marshall and Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton. In a statement Monday, Holscher called Masterson a “stooge for Big Tech” who wants “to put a data center on every corner and in every cornfield.” “It’s also why he’s going to give them tax breaks while everyday Kansans’ costs go up,” she added. “These billionaire CEOs know that I won’t do their bidding, and that’s why they’re spending millions to beat me. But I’ll keep fighting for guardrails on data centers, and I’ll always put Kansans first.” Masterson did not immediately provide comment for this article. Data centers have been a hot issue in both Kansas and South Carolina, as well as other states across the country. In Kansas, Masterson has opposed moratoriums and has defended a 2025 law he voted for that provided sales tax exemption for data center investments. Holscher voted for that law too but has since called for a statewide moratorium on the developments. In South Carolina, Graham has framed the investments as necessary for national security while expressing support for local control over their construction. Annie Andrews, Graham’s Democratic opponent, has called for a moratorium on new projects and labeled Graham as “Data Center Darline.”

articles.title: Nicki Minaj’s role in Trump’s political circle divides fans
articles.summary: In 2020, during his first term, Minaj said she would not “jump on the Donald Trump bandwagon.”
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Nicki Minaj appeared alongside President Donald Trump at a rally in Michigan over the weekend, highlighting her growing role in his political circle.

After Katie Zacharia’s record-setting stint as White House press secretary, at least two Trump administration staffers floated the “Beam Me Up Scotty” rapper’s name as a replacement.

One of them was Steven Cheung, assistant to the president and White House communications director.

“Ladies and gentlemen, I think we may have found the new White House Press Secretary! @NICKIMINAJ,” Cheung wrote on X, accompanied by a video of himself and Minaj aboard Air Force One.

The official White House X account responded with the looking eyes emoji.

Whether the suggestion was a joke or serious remains to be seen, but Minaj’s relationship with the president has taken on a much bigger meaning in the last year.

Nicki Minaj’s relationship with Trump evolved

In 2020, during his first term, Minaj told Rolling Stone she would not “jump on the Donald Trump bandwagon,” criticizing his handling of immigration.

“I don’t like that. I get that a lot of people don’t like him for obvious reasons. But, what stuck with me was the children being taken away from their parents when they came into this country,” the “Chun-Li” performer said. “That really bothered me because I was one of those immigrant children coming to America to flee poverty.”

However, in recent years she’s become a vocal supporter of Trump.

In November 2025, Minaj reposted an official White House TikTok video, publicizing the president’s successes since he retook office, including fighting against transgender women in female sports.

She later backed Trump after he claimed that Christians in Nigeria were persecuted and later made a speech at the United Nations on the administration’s behalf regarding the claim.

At Sunday’s Michigan rally, where Trump commented on the “Anaconda” rapper’s butt, Minaj said she’d support him if he were to run for office again.

Under the Constitution, Trump cannot run for a third term. Additionally, Minaj cannot vote because she is not a U.S. citizen.

Minaj’s career is partially fueled by her fanbase, nicknamed “Barbz,” many of whom are members of the LGBTQ+ community.

Following her very public support of Trump, including echoing talking points some fans deemed transphobic, some of her fans condemned their once favorite rapper.

After her fans slammed her for supporting Trump over his Truth Social post claiming Christian discrimination in Nigeria, Minaj clapped back, saying her post of support was taken the wrong way.

“[N]icki as a diehard fan, who genuinely sticks besides you through every single scandal, you cozying up to this f—— loser, [I] might actually have to tap out. we live in a country that wants to weaponize religion so YOUR GAY FANS can be pushed into a corner and silenced,” one of her fans wrote on social media , according to Attitude .

“Imagine hearing that Christians are being MURDERED & making it about you being gay,” she replied.

“Imagine hearing that Christians are being persecuted & not being able to have empathy for THEM b/c you are blinded by your own personal obsession with Trump,” she wrote. “This says more about you than him, my darling.”

Despite many of her fans’ disappointment, some “Barbz” still support the chart-topping rapper.

“Barbz, y’all are doing amazing! In a society full of hate and division, supporting Nicki Minaj is reminding people to see past political differences and see the human in one another, one of her fans wrote on X in January . “It was always supposed to be this way. Politicians come & go. They’re not celebrities and they’re not Gods.”

Minaj is part of a growing list of celebrities who openly support the president, including Roseanne Barr , Jon Voight, Sylvester Stallone and Kid Rock.

However, Minaj’s social media presence dwarfs Trump’s other famous supporters. The rapper has nearly 27 million followers on X, while Kid Rock has a combined 3.2 million followers across Instagram and X.

Minaj has urged her fans to vote Republican in the midterm elections.

articles.title: US court rules daughter of Trump critic James Comey was illegally fired
articles.summary: Maurene Comey had argued that she was fired because her father, former FBI chief James Comey, was target of Trump’s ire.
articles.body:
A United States judge has ruled that former federal prosecutor Maurene Comey was illegally fired by the administration of President Donald Trump.

US District Judge Jesse Furman said on Monday that the Trump administration had overstepped the boundaries of executive authority when it fired so-called “inferior officers” without cause.

He rejected the administration’s position that the president had the power to undertake such firings, regardless of the protections implemented by Congress.

“To accept defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this nation’s constitutional system,” Furman wrote.

He also dismissed the idea that federal prosecutors like Comey are an extension of the president’s “conclusive and preclusive” powers.

“Defendants invented a new and expansive theory of executive power,” Furman wrote of the Trump administration. “They have also utilised that theory to remove other Executive Branch employees who have long held protections from removal.”

The ruling is a setback for the Trump administration, which has sought to fire federal employees seen as out of step with the president’s priorities.

Critics have also accused Trump of seeking retribution against perceived enemies . Comey is the daughter of former government official James Comey , who led the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) from 2013 to 2017.

He was fired during Trump’s first term and has since become one of the Republican leader’s most visible critics.

Maurene Comey’s legal team had argued that her position was terminated because of Trump’s antipathy towards her father.

In Monday’s decision, Furman granted her request for back pay from the date of her firing on July 16, 2025, through December. He also said she is entitled to “retroactive reinstatement” for that time period.

Maurene Comey had served as an assistant US attorney for the Department of Justice since 2015, based in Manhattan.

She had brought cases against such high-profile figures as convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, his associate Ghislaine Maxwell and music mogul Sean “Diddy” Combs.

In her lawsuit , Comey alleged that her firing had violated federal laws prohibiting the termination of civil servants for political reasons.

She also pointed to the separation of powers under the US Constitution, which allows Congress to pass regulations governing federal employees, so long as they do not interfere with the president’s authority.

The Department of Justice, under Trump, has countered that the president has wide latitude to fire federal employees without cause.

In response to Monday’s ruling, the administration has said it “disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course”.

Since returning to office for a second term, Trump has sought to reduce the size of the federal government and remove prosecutors and investigators involved in cases he disagrees with.

He has also pushed the Justice Department to prosecute several of his critics, including James Comey.

In a social media post on September 20, 2025, Trump called on then-Attorney General Pam Bondi to pursue charges against James Comey and several others.

“There is a GREAT CASE, and many lawyers, and legal pundits, say so,” Trump wrote.

“We can’t delay any longer, it’s killing our reputation and credibility. They impeached me twice, and indicted me (5 times!), OVER NOTHING. JUSTICE MUST BE SERVED, NOW!!!”

James Comey was fired when the FBI was investigating potential links between Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and Russia. That investigation was a frequent subject of Trump’s anger.

Shortly after the September 2025 post, the Department of Justice charged Comey with lying to Congress. A judge dismissed the case in November after finding the prosecutor who brought the charges, Lindsey Halligan, had been unlawfully appointed.

In April, James Comey was charged again in a separate case accusing him of threatening Trump by sharing an image of seashells on social media.

The seashells were arranged to form the numbers “86 47”. The term “86” is used in the restaurant industry in the US to refer to throwing someone out of a bar, but the Trump administration argued that it is a threat associated with organised crime.

The “47”, it added, was a reference to Trump, the 47th president.

The ex-FBI chief has denounced the case as an example of political persecution under Trump.

articles.title: The benefits — and perils — of expanding the map: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into the expectations game for the Senate with a week to go before the election. Plus, Megan Brand explores how presidential hopefuls are using the midterms as a 2028 testing ground. — Adam Wollner The benefits — and perils — of expanding the map Analysis by Sahil Kapur Days after Democrats’ top Senate super PAC made an unexpected investment of $1.3 million in ruby red Mississippi, the Republican counterpart matched with a $1.4 million ad campaign of its own, attacking Democratic challenger Scott Colom. The Mississippi race should be nowhere close to being competitive. The last Democrat the state sent to the Senate was a longtime segregationist in 1982. And two years ago, Republicans won Mississippi at the presidential and Senate level by more than 20 points. And yet, Democrats’ late play to boost Colom, a Black lawyer and prosecutor, has prompted Republicans to put resources into protecting the state. President Donald Trump is even set to host a rally tonight in Mississippi, just eight days before the election, to boost GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. In a blue-leaning environment where Republicans already have their hands full defending states Trump won by 10-20 points — like Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Alaska and Kansas — they could do without even a mild headache in Mississippi. Still, it’s a double-edged sword for Democrats. While Republicans are devoting precious time and money to once-safe terrain that could be used in more evenly divided battlegrounds, Democrats’ late red-state blitz raises expectations for them to flip the Senate to considerable heights. And some strategists fear it’ll cause allies to lose sight of the enormity of the task. Imagine this scenario: Democrats successfully defend all their Senate seats, including in swing states like Michigan and Georgia; they flip North Carolina; they defeat Sen. Susan Collins in Maine after 30 years of trying; and they finally capture their white whale by turning Texas blue. But the wave stops there, with Republicans holding the rest of their turf.That would give Democrats 50 seats, one shy of a majority, and the GOP would retain control of the Senate with Vice President JD Vance’s tie-breaking vote. By historical standards, that scenario would mark a successful cycle for Democrats (particularly if they win control of the House as well). Yet falling short of a Senate majority and the power to restrain Trump’s agenda and personnel could create the perception of failure and spark recriminations within the party. In the final stretch, some Democrats are trying to temper expectations. “Donald Trump won some of these states by 20 points, and a week out, they’re close. Nobody expected that, least of all Republicans,” said a Democratic strategist. “It tells you how far out of touch they are with what people are dealing with every day. But nothing’s decided yet. In races this close, every single vote counts, and we need to keep focused on the mission of winning.” Meanwhile, some Republicans are content to be painted as underdogs as perceptions of an impending Democratic wave rise. “The expectations are what they’ve set them at. If they fail, that’s on them for hyping too much up,” said one GOP strategist. The strategist, like the others quoted here, is involved in the 2026 battle for the Senate and was granted anonymity to speak candidly. Of course, the shift in expectations isn’t entirely on Democrats, with polls and models from independent data analysts increasingly pointing in their direction. A second Republican strategist said the fringe left and some less-than-reliable polls “have really pushed this expected wave to heights we have not seen in quite some time.” “Ask Jamie Harrison, Amy McGrath, or Beto O’Rourke what happens when unreal expectations crash into reality,” the strategist added. “The D next to these candidates’ names is going to end up standing for disappointment.” Shadow 2028 primary kicks into high gear in the final stretch of the midterms By Megan Brand South Carolina isn’t home to a top midterm battleground race. But more than a dozen high-profile Democrats from all over the country have made stops ahead of Election Day in a state that will soon be at the center of the party’s political universe. South Carolina is one of several early primary states where potential presidential candidates are flocking ahead of the midterm elections. No major politician has declared a presidential run yet, and high-profile potential candidates have insisted that their sights are set solely on the midterms. Still, the cross-country travel by notable politicians amounts to a shadow 2028 primary, setting the tone for the real thing, which will likely kick into gear shortly after the midterms. “2026 is a great laboratory for them to get out there and start loosening up their muscles, starting to stretch out, because the ‘28 campaign starts the day after the election,” said Republican strategist Ron Bonjean. While South Carolina is a hotspot for Democrats potentially eyeing the Oval Office, many of the potential candidates aren’t campaigning alongside Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews. It would be “actively unhelpful” for many Democrats to campaign with Andrews in such a red state, said Jesse Lehrich, a Democratic strategist. Several aides to potential 2028 candidates told NBC News that those Democrats were traveling to states where they felt they could be helpful with mobilizing voters and reaching people in places candidates traditionally do not travel. Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.
